item.title: Healing from Trauma is Natural
item.description:
Trauma

Healing from Trauma is Natural

We have been convinced that traumatic experiences are life sentences. Why?

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Traumatic experiences have been presented to us as life sentences that require extensive interventions.
  • However, this flies in the face of decades of research that finds humans to be reliably resilient.
  • Reframing potentially traumatic events through the lens of up-to-date resilience research can free all of us.
Source: Deborah Radeka / Pixabay

This post is Part 2 of a series.

As you may have seen in your social media feeds and in pop psychology books, trauma healing has become big business. We could even call it an industry or an industrial complex at this point.

The language of this industry is everywhere, and we're all being "triggered," or "moving into fight and flight," or "regulating our nervous systems," or "hacking our parasympathetic" or engaging in "trauma-informed" trainings.

All this in-language could be seen as a positive movement, but what I'm seeing—as a survivor of serious childhood abuse, and as a researcher—concerns me. As I wrote in part 1 of this series, decades of research has shown that fully two thirds of us will regain our resilience after traumatic incidents—of any intensity or duration—without the need for interventions of any kind. No therapy, no nervous system hacking, no trauma-informed anything.

It is, in other words, natural for us to recover from injuries and traumas, and it is natural for us to restabilize ourselves. And for the one third of us who experience enduring post-traumatic difficulties, there are research-backed ways to help us regain our stability and resilience.

The Protective Power of the Flexibility Mindset

In researcher George Bonanno's book, The End of Trauma, we learn that humans are a remarkably resilient species. In one of the many surprising findings Dr. Bonanno shares, we learn about a mindset that the two thirds of people who recover their resilience tend to share; it's called the flexibility mindset:

At the core of the mindset are three interrelated beliefs: optimism about the future, confidence in our ability to cope, and a willingness to think about a threat as a challenge (Bonanno, 2021, p. 123).

My concern about much of today's trauma-healing industry is that it tends to get in the way of all three of these essential and protective beliefs.

Instead of optimism about the future, we trauma survivors are warned about the haunting symptoms that may show up years, decades, or even generations after we face traumatic events. Instead of instilling confidence in our natural ability to regain our resilience, we are given a list of dire aftereffects and even the ACES (adverse childhood experiences) quiz that predicts the symptoms and diseases children will allegedly develop after traumatic incidents. And instead of helping us see potentially traumatizing events as challenges, we are invited to see them as catastrophic situations that damage our bodies, our emotions, our nervous systems, our capacity for social engagement, and even our cranial nerves.

article continues after advertisement

None of that is true for everyone. In fact, considering the resilience trajectory that 66.6 percent of us follow, we're twice as likely to regain our resilience after traumatic events than we are to have lasting symptoms.

Trauma is Not an Entity That Forces a Specific Outcome

In The End of Trauma, Dr. Bonanno helps us see that trauma is not an entity over which we are powerless bystanders (or victims). Instead, he refers to "potentially traumatic events," which is a bit clunky to write out, but also a very important distinction.

A potentially traumatic event does not force me to become damaged, as if I am a nonliving item upon which the troubles of the world are engraved. We cannot responsibly say that X amount of potentially traumatic events will create Y amount of symptoms; that's overreach, and it sends a terrible message to people like me who faced serious traumatic situations from childhood through early adulthood.

Because depending on the event or situation, I may or may not develop enduring post-traumatic symptoms. In many cases, I may recover quickly, or I may require a period of healing and readjustment; it's deeply individual. The traumatic incident doesn't determine my outcome; I do. I have agency, flexibility, and an inborn capacity for healing.

But we can say that no matter the length or intensity of potentially traumatic events, two thirds of us will regain our resilience, because we are not mere victims or bystanders. We are living, capable organisms who bring 200,000 years of homo sapiens survival skills to bear on every situation we face.

Trauma isn't an entity that causes specific injuries or difficulties; it is a destabilizing situation we experience as whole beings who are a part of an astonishingly resilient species.

Reclaiming the Language of Resilience

I read Dr. Bonanno's book as I was preparing the 2023 update of my book, The Language of Emotions, and in a final edit, I searched my manuscript for the word trauma. Thank goodness I did, because I had presented trauma as a kind of entity throughout the book. I had bad sentences such as: "When traumas occur..."—as if potentially traumatic events would always cause endless suffering.

article continues after advertisement

Since then, I've been aware of the ways that we unnecessarily typecast trauma survivors and surround them with outdated and melodramatic frames that may restrict their natural movements into flexibility and resilience.

At this time, when many trauma healing modalities are being called into question, it's important to make sure that our approaches are going to lead survivors somewhere valuable. Through our language, our references, and our approaches, we can either frame trauma survivors as damaged victims, or we can help them develop the flexibility mindset that leads to healing and recovery.

Because regardless of the length, type, or intensity of potentially traumatic events, healing from trauma is natural.

Coming next in part 3: The strange and surprising features of the flexibility mindset.

item.title: What Happens When AI Adapts to Us
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What Happens When AI Adapts to Us

Exploring artificial intelligence (AI), adaptation, and human relationships

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI, when used appropriately within limits, can benefit from some human abilities, including creativity.
  • Overuse of AI is linked to decreased creativity and critical thinking.
  • The overuse of technology has been associated with decreased empathy.
  • The more we rely upon AI and technology, the more it shapes our behavior.

In Part I of this blog, I discussed how AI affects attachment, empathy, and vulnerability in human relationships (Hoffman, 2026). In Part II, I explore how technology adapts to us, and how we adapt to technology. These adaptations have vital implications for what it means to be human and how we grow and evolve individually and collectively.

The Dangers of AI Adapting to Us

AI is often sycophantic or overly agreeable (see Hoffman & Hoffman, 2026). An extreme of this was seen with GPT-4o, which at times reinforced and even encouraged distorted or delusional thoughts and considerations of risky behaviors. People were quickly becoming overly reliant on it, with this dependence discouraging critical thinking and potentially contributing to mental health risks. Over-validation and agreement are the primary reasons people became overly attached to it. While later versions have partially addressed these issues, concerns remain.

AI platforms adapt responses partially based on what they know about us. For example, at a holiday party in 2025, I was discussing AI with several friends who are also existential therapists. During our conversation, I asked ChatGPT to give a professional description of several of us to see what it knew. We found it amusing, and sometimes worrisome.

A few weeks later, while reviewing conference proposals, several described the presenter as an emerging leader in existential psychology. Curious, I asked ChatGPT who it identified as the most influential emerging leaders in existential psychology. Most of those whom I asked AI to write a bio for a few weeks earlier appeared at the top of the list. When I then asked it to answer the same question disregarding the history of my inquiries, only one of these individuals was listed as a leading emerging figure, and she appeared lower on the list. ChatGPT shaped its answers around what it appeared likely I would like as a response. This is similar to the sycophantic qualities of AI.

Source: Louis Hoffman, Ph.D.

Even as it adapts to us, we are conforming to AI, often without recognizing it. There is a potential for AI to push us in a direction of becoming more alike, losing aspects of our uniqueness. As AI revises our emails, text messages, letters, and even papers, we are losing the originality of our writing and communication.

As we draw from sources that AI deems appropriate, we are increasingly reliant on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) sources of information that are not representative of many cultural ways of knowing and are narrowing our epistemological diversity. This also reflects a likely bias toward quantitative research, which emphasizes shared patterns and commonalities across individuals, over qualitative research, which seeks to understand subjective experience, contextual meaning, and the uniqueness of persons. However, both ways of knowing are essential for advancing knowledge.

The Loss of Relational Skills

In an article with Lakoda Hoffman, after reviewing the literature, we argued that while AI could potentially have some benefits for creativity, critical thinking, and even empathy if used well, over-reliance on AI seems to negatively impact all of these vital aspects of being human and our engagement as a productive member of society (Hoffman & Hoffman, 2026). When relationships become too wired through inserting technology into relationships, or when technology replaces essential parts of human relationships and community, there are social and psychological consequences.

The ease and accessibility of AI make it easy to become overly reliant on it, even if one begins with good intentions about using it with greater constraint. To avoid the dangers of AI, it is vital that we not only learn to use it well but also develop the self-discipline to avoid over-usage and other problems associated with it. We, too, must not neglect the development of important interpersonal skills and qualities, such as empathy and compassion, that we need as humans.

What happens when, potentially in the near future, therapists have earbuds listening in on conversations and advising us what therapeutic technique to use? And couples have earbuds guiding them in their arguments? These, it seems, may not be far into the future. While there may be short-term benefits associated with such advances, there is a loss of humanity that accompanies it. With advances such as this, we may no longer be developing, refining, and evolving our personal skills individually and collectively. Instead, we will move in the direction of becoming the technology.

Conclusion

AI has implications for the human experience and potentially even what it means to be human. It is imperative that we develop healthy ways to live with it. This is more than merely learning how to use it effectively and efficiently. It also entails recognizing the negative implications of poor usage and over-reliance on fundamental aspects of the human experience.

The way we relate as humans is rapidly evolving as technology, and AI in particular, evolves. As Kirk Schneider (2019) stated, “The more we court machines, the more machine-like we become” (p. 36). Fundamental aspects of human relationships are withering away as human attachments, community, and seeking support through close relationships are replaced with attachments to technology and pursuing emotional support through interaction with AI. Many are no longer developing and utilizing foundational relational qualities. There are aspects of humanity and human relationships that are threatened by the way we use AI—and these fundamental parts of our humanity, including empathy, compassion, vulnerability, critical thinking, and creativity, are worth preserving.

item.title: Should You Correct Someone Who Misspeaks? It Depends
item.description:
Media

Should You Correct Someone Who Misspeaks? It Depends

Knowing when to speak up, and when silence is golden.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Correction with civility is linked with positive relationship-related outcomes.
  • Tone matters: uncivil correction has negative consequences.
  • Correction is more likely to be successful if it comes from a good friend.
  • Public correction on social media may be uniquely damaging to the poster.

Your spouse mistakenly gives inaccurate directions to the airport where someone is rushing to catch a flight. Your ride share driver boldly misstates the purpose of a drug you prescribe frequently as a physician. Which of these people do you correct—and how?

When necessary and done gracefully, correction is valuable and can strengthen relationships. Yet in addition to time and place, tone matters too. The type of correction that comes under scrutiny most often is the kind that makes others uncomfortable because it is public, embarrassing, or even humiliating. Yet for people who merely want to be helpful, without alienating the person being corrected, where is the line? Research has some helpful tips.

Source: Image by rawpixel from Pixabay

Public Correction: Harmful or Helpful?

Raffael Heiss et al. (2025) examined the impact of peer correction of alleged misinformation on social media platforms.[i] Focusing on the impact of civility, they investigated how tone matters to the person being corrected and determines relational outcomes. They found that civil correction was linked with more success and positive relationship-related outcomes, while uncivil correction had negative consequences.

Regarding what type of people use what form of correction, Heiss et al. found that people who have a higher education are more likely to engage in civil correction attempts, often through education in media literacy, respectful language, and logical argumentation. On social media, correctors may augment information with graphical content or methods of presenting complex ideas through short-form posts.

Yet generally, Heiss et al. note that correcting other people is a delicate decision considering its potential to create conflict and stressful situations. It is more likely to be successful, they explain, if it comes from a good friend, includes trustworthy sources, and does not interfere with the beliefs of the person being corrected.

Civility Reduces Negativity

Heiss et al. recognize that corrections are risky because they may be viewed as an attack against the speaker’s deeply held beliefs, opinions, ideology, or view of the world. They acknowledge that while some people appreciate correction and respond positively, other people view corrections as evidence of negative views, which can strain a relationship. Some may actually view correction as a personal attack and become defensive, which can further reduce relational quality.

Heiss et al. recognize that public correction on social media may be uniquely damaging to the recipient who is made to feel embarrassed. Yet a tone of civility is helpful. Citing a previous study (Bode et al., 2020) which examined uncivil, neutral, or civil corrections on social media, they acknowledge that an “affirmative tone” can make correction easier for both the corrector and the person being corrected.

article continues after advertisement

Correcting with civility allows people to rectify misinformation and maintain relationships in the process. Heiss et al. found that uncivil correction enhanced negative relationship consequences both directly and indirectly through experiencing failure. And regarding topics, they warn that uncivil correction can promote polarization around hot button topics such as health or politics—which could be amplified through negative social consequences.

Correct With Care

Whomever decides to speak up in the face of known misinformation should remember that although correction may in some cases be necessary, it is socially risky and should be carried out with care. Civil correction and redirection with a motive to educate not embarrass can mitigate negativity and maintain relationships.

item.title: 4 Reasons Confusion Signals Psychological Maturity
item.description:
Openness

4 Reasons Confusion Signals Psychological Maturity

Confusion suggests potential for continued psychological growth.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Confusion indicates awareness and tolerance of complexity in ourselves and others.
  • Confusion supports integration over reductionism.
  • Confusion is a natural aspect of intellectual humility.
  • Confusion suggests personal security.

My toddler, my most respected mentors, and my therapy patients in a process of profound growth all have something in common—their ability to look at things with an open mind and a capacity to experience confusion long enough to expand and deepen their understanding of themselves and the world around them.

If asked to imagine an individual who is secure in themselves, intelligent, and even wise, “confused” may seem an odd quality to mention, let alone prioritize. Yet, the ability to be confused can be an important sign of psychological maturity.

1. Confusion indicates awareness and tolerance of complexity in ourselves and others

Confusion is a natural emotion we experience when pieces of information don’t add up. Here, “information” can be defined broadly — as in literal facts that are hard to imagine being true at the same time, but also experiences, like how we feel, what we want, and the choices we make. For instance, we might experience both wanting and resisting something or having both loving and angry feelings toward a loved one. However, we can only experience confusion if we recognize those pieces of information and attempt to hold them in awareness at the same time—a useful, if not essential, skill for navigating the numerous scenarios which may evoke internal conflict and confusion. In reality, there are many cases where we are conveniently unaware of contradictions and are spared the uncomfortable feelings that would otherwise rise to the surface, like confusion.

Confusion can feel uncomfortable for a number of reasons. The introduction of complex or seemingly contradictory information can challenge a previously held or wished-for belief. In these cases, confusion is a close friend to fear, where a challenge to perception may be experienced as a personal or existential threat.

2. Confusion supports integration over reductionism

One “solution” to the discomfort of confusion is to do away with the interloping data, to dismiss it or rationalize it to the extent that it has no impact on the prior conclusion or belief system. This is just as much a pitfall in clinical practice as it is in our personal lives. Having worked extensively on interdisciplinary psychiatric teams, it is undeniable that good care rests on a comprehensive understanding of the person who is participating in treatment, which requires a commitment to integrating information gathered from multiple viewpoints and areas of expertise (including the patient’s experience). One must integrate various pieces of information amid the temptation to dismiss information that presents a more complicated or uncertain picture. The task of integration still typically involves organizing (and reorganizing) each piece of information into a hierarchy and searching for the best whole picture that accommodates the data in the most sensible way. In this way, integration also requires some interpretation, taking the stance that, “If we are to assume that all of this somehow fits together, how can we understand each piece in a way that makes that possible?”

article continues after advertisement

3. Confusion is a natural aspect of intellectual humility

Commitment to integration requires patience and the capacity to tolerate “not knowing,” both in the present and beyond. When attempting to genuinely understand ourselves, others, and the world, we evidence psychological maturity by accepting that our best efforts will rarely, if ever, produce certain and unchangeable points of view. Openness to learning more and being wrong often invites experiences of confusion, and tolerating confusion allows us to be curious, thus driving the continued pursuit of meaningful understanding. Again, applied to mental health practice, solo practitioners ought not be deemed ineffectual merely because they don’t have access to an interdisciplinary team; rather they are most reliable when they acknowledge the limits of what they know, keeping an open, wondering ear to whatever information makes its way into the consulting room, careful not to assume that they have the whole picture at any point in time. Spoiler: neither solo providers nor well-oiled and resourced interdisciplinary teams ever have the whole picture.

4. Confusion suggests a level of personal security

While openness is an important aspect of maturity, lacking any “backbone” entirely would be as problematic as being overly rigid. Just as dismissing new information may be one way to avoid confusion (and sacrifice sophistication), abandoning old information may occur for the same purpose. We often feel confused when we occupy the tension between openness to new perspectives and reasonable commitment to what we already think and believe, holding prior knowledge and new information with even, discerning hands as opposed to reactively abandoning old beliefs and experiences.

Conclusion and application to therapy

In therapy (or in any moment), when a person recognizes feelings of confusion, especially around painful, deeply held, or quickly assumed beliefs about themselves, others, or the world, that may actually be a good sign, an indication of openness, and an earnest opportunity for learning. Rather than a patient or a therapist jumping in too early to “clear up” the confusion, there is benefit to letting it sit. Sorting through it together over time supports an organic process of psychological growth. Not only does this promote affective tolerance, but it supports curiosity and mutual discovery, where neither a therapist nor the patient presumes to know beyond what is knowable at that moment, but both are committed to the pursuit of meaningful, grounded understanding.

item.title: Postpartum Pet Aversion: What Is It and How Can We Help?
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Postpartum Pet Aversion: What Is It and How Can We Help?

Pregnant or new mothers may suddenly feel repulsed by their pets; it's fixable.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Hormones don't make mothers reject pets.
  • PPA is not maternal instinct.
  • This doesn't mean that you no longer love your pet.
  • PPA should not be ignored.

Postpartum Pet Aversion (PPA) is a condition in which a new mother may suddenly experience feelings of disgust, rage, hatred, or fear of their previously beloved pet. Although this happens more often after the birth of a child, it can also occur peripartum (before the birth of the child, while the woman is still pregnant). Although this condition is not very common, it can happen to anyone, and so it helps to understand why it happens, how to prevent PPA, and how to deal with the condition if it does develop.

Source: Photo by Picsea on Unsplash

Explanation

Postpartum Pet Aversion (PPA) is usually the result of stress and a caregiving burden. There is no evidence that it is biological (hormonal). In fact, biology shows the opposite effect. Spending time with pets raises our oxytocin levels (the hormone that bonds a mother to their baby, romantic partner, or pet) and lowers our stress hormones, most notably cortisol. But a new baby arriving can cause sleep disruption, physical recovery, identity changes, reduced time and financial strain. In addition the mother can experience social isolation and significant anxiety regarding the safety of the baby.

Not all pregnancies are comfortable, and during a difficult pregnancy a mother can also experience chronic pain and fatigue. Taking care of a pet's daily needs can seem like an additional burden when a mother's capacity to cope is already low. Childbirth and hormones are not known to influence PPA, but chronic stress and feelings of being overwhelmed are the most likely cause. In addition, mothers can experience Compassion Fatigue — they are already caring for their baby and perhaps other children, a partner, or older adults, and they simply use up all their caring and there is little left for the family pet.

This may manifest in various ways — rage, anger, frustration, not wanting the pet to be near them, hating the smell or feel of their pet, or anger towards barking or other pet vocalizations. When a mother is stressed, physically uncomfortable, and depressed, a pet's normal sensory and caregiving demands may start to feel aversive. This is most likely due to a defense mechanism known as Displacement — the mother feels that it is less socially acceptable to feel frustrated with a crying baby than a needy dog, so they turn their frustration towards their pet. The anger has to go somewhere and the mother's psyche aims it towards the one being who is least able to complain.

The anxiety and stress that the mother feels may also result in feelings of guilt and shame, because this previously was a beloved pet, and cause her to question her capability as a mother. Guilt can intensify this cycle. The parent may withdraw from their pet because the care feels overwhelming, but then feel ashamed about the withdraw which then makes the distress more intense and makes interacting with their pet even more difficult. Research shows that limited social support and practical caregiving help, housing or financial insecurity, and difficulty meeting pet-care needs are more closely tied with negative experiences.

article continues after advertisement

A pet's behavior can also change during pregnancy and after the birth, because of routine disruptions, unfamiliar sounds and smells, reduced attention, and the appearance of new people (guest, family members, nanny or nurse). A pet may become more clingy, vigilant, avoidant, make more noise, or may become more reactive or destructive — these behaviors may in turn add to the parent's distress. It's important to note that this situation is bi-directional, not simply a mother rejecting a pet.

It is important to make sure that during the pregnancy — before the birth of the child — new routines are established with the pet that allows them to feel more integrated in the new family structure, rather than marginalized. When parents wait until after the birth to change routines, jealousy and misunderstanding may occur. For example, a dog who sleeps on the bed each night but then, after the birth, is suddenly told they cannot, may (understandable) act with confusion and jealousy towards a new child. It is important to not only integrate the family pet into the new routines before the birth, but after the birth to continue to treat the pet with the love and attention that they are used to afterwards.

If the new mother is unable to do this, a partner or family member can assist in caregiving tasks to alleviate the burden on the new mother and allow more positive (not task driven) interactions with the mother and pet. The family may want to seek out a positive reinforcement or force-free trainer to help establish a new routine with their pet. Alternately, if the pet develops behavioral issues, pet meds (like Prozac) may help. (It's important to only work with positive reinforcement or force-free trainers, since the introduction of aversive methods in training can accidentally make a pet more aggressive towards a child).

article continues after advertisement

Most importantly, PPA is a clinically relevant warning sign of broader distress, including the devolution of the new mother into postpartum depression or even psychosis. If the PPA occurs with persistent sadness, panic, rage, intrusive thoughts, inability to sleep (when given the chance), hopelessness or helplessness, or trouble caring for herself or the baby, it is imperative that the mother seek help for Postpartum Depression. A trauma history, or a history of a disrupted attachment in the mother's childhood, can also contribute to the development of PPA or Postpartum Depression (PD). If a mother already questions her ability to care for a child, then an inability to care for her pet may cause her to question her abilities as a mother and her identity as a mother. She may spiral into a web of confusion over whether she is able to care for any living being.

Source: Photo by Jack van Tricht on Unsplash

Key Points

It's important to remember that:

  • Hormones don't make mothers reject pets — it actually is the opposite!
  • PPA is not maternal instinct — although the mother may feel protective towards the new baby, many mothers feel protective towards a new baby and their other children, or pets.
  • This doesn't mean that you no longer love your pet — feelings can shift under acute strain, and reaching caregiving capacity can make anyone irritable. This is not about love but about being pushed to the limit. The good news is that the change in feelings of attachment is most likely temporary.
  • PPA should not be ignored — severe anger, neglect, risk, thoughts of harming yourself or others, require immediate support.

Clinical Treatment

It's important to address the practical strain rather than the emotion. I would not suggest rehoming your pet, since this may reinforce feelings of guilt, incapacity, and depression. In addition, the rehoming of a pet may cause other children in the house to question whether they will also get rehomed (or abandoned) if they become a burden. Instead, solicit the help of friends and family to help alleviate the caregiving burden. Stick to predictable pet routines when feasible and recruit concrete help for walks, cleaning, training and vet visits.

Social support for pet and child care, boundaries for pet-child interactions and realistic expectation-setting are the most helpful factors in getting past PPA (note: you can have healthy pet-child boundaries while keeping your pet integrated in the family, although you should always keep new babies and pets separated when not supervised). Working weekly with a mental health clinician can help a mother explore their feelings of postpartum depression, identity, guilt, shame, compassion fatigue, and postpartum pet aversion. This is the recommended treatment, in addition to social supports to alleviate caregiving burden. PPA can be treated and will go away, but it is important to seek help when needed.

Disclaimer: If your feelings are severe, escalating, or paired with depression, anxiety, intrusive thoughts, rage, or inability to function, please contact your ob/gyn, primary care doctor or a mental health clinician. If you feel there is an immediate risk of harm to yourself, the baby or your pet please call 911 or go to your nearest emergency room.

item.title: Consent Is Not an Alibi
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Consent Is Not an Alibi

Personal Perspective: The real question about cage fighting is why we watch.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Most sport risks injury as a side effect. In cage fighting, the harm is the product.
  • Consent explains why a fighter steps in. It does not explain why an audience member buys a ticket.
  • Dignity means no person should become an instrument of someone else's entertainment.
  • The ethical question sits with the spectator, not only the promoters and fighters.

As a teenage male, I was very attracted to boxing. My dad, an athlete himself, always motivated me and my siblings to practice some level of physical activity. When I sought permission to box, my mom’s response was, “You want to pay so people can punch your face?” I was sure that my father would give me permission, though, and that his affection for athletics would convince my mom. His response: “The goal of athletics can never be to cause physical harm to another human being or animal.”

No, I couldn’t box.

I know today that you can practice boxing safely without ever punching another human being. But at that time and in our neighborhood, this was not an option. I know that being able to defend and protect yourself or others is important and requires training and hard work, including accepting that you will cause or receive physical harm. I also know that almost all kinds of sports can cause injuries to yourself, your teammates, or your opponents. However, in other sports, physical injuries are typically an unintended consequence and not the goal.

So I ask, which understanding of social life and human dignity would allow that people enter a “cage” and beat each other bloody? We call this type of fighting a sport today, but when the explicit aim is systematic trauma, the distinction between athleticism and spectacle collapses. We have evolved enough to know that bloodshed is not bravery. We have laws against assault in the street. Why, then, do we celebrate it when it is televised and sold (not to mention, often scripted and choreographed)?

If dignity means anything, it must mean that no human being is a tool for another’s entertainment—especially not through measured violence. When we pay to watch faces swell and bones crack, we are not celebrating the human spirit. We are paying for permission to forget that the person in the cage is someone’s child, someone’s father, someone’s self—reduced to a gladiator for our weekend thrill.

Let’s not pretend that consent erases the ethical question. Consent explains the contract, but does not justify the culture. The question isn’t whether they agreed but why we feel entitled to watch.
